s2.p1: No WDSF member federation: Oceania’s only two are **Australia** and **New Zealand**. We found no record of a ballroom or Latin school or competition here.
s2.p2: Music and dance are among Nauru’s most popular forms of expression, often at **festivals and celebrations**. But ==the written record we found is thin==.

s3.p: ended the dance. Under colonial-era **1936 rules**, the district constable had to sound his shell, the dobwu, on dancing days: Wednesdays, Saturdays, secular holidays.

s4.p1: Not dance, but hands. Nauru’s string figures are among the **most complex in the world**. Many, called kawada, go back to contests among young men.
s4.p2: Nauruan strings ran **over 4.5 metres**, against the usual 1.8. Honor Maude’s ==1971 book== gathered well over a hundred figures.

s5.name: DOGOROPA
s5.p: Once a **religious ritual** to call nine gods of ancient Nauru, per the Expo 2012 blog. In **1994**, ten 11-year-olds from Nauru danced it in Fukuoka, Japan.

s5.name: FRIGATE BIRD
s5.p: Sixth-graders from Nauru Primary School presented it at the **Festival of Pacific Arts**: boys clapped and sang, girls portrayed the birds’ flight and perching.

s6.p: “Strictly forbidden” by the colonial-era Administrator in **1936**. Men attending had to carry lamps. Penalty: 10 shillings, up to a month in jail, or both.

s7.p: On Nauru’s National Day at **Expo 2012 Yeosu**, in Korea, the **Yaren Youth Group** performed the Dogoropa in the Expo Hall.
s7.p2: Nauru is due in Belgrade. In January 2026, the Expo’s site listed ==among its best-known dances== Ekawada, Dogoropwa, Itti and Anabar amin keramon.
